extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agency staff, CWG authors, and policymakers reviewing climate assessment reports (notice-and-comment participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and substantive criteria for assessing the scientific and economic soundness of a climate assessment or policy-report (here, the Draft CWG Report), including treatment of biophysical impacts, agronomy, ocean change, and economic valuation (SCC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of CO2 fertilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Note existence of CO2 fertilization (leaf-level photosynthetic response) but do not let it obscure net harms from rising CO2 and other greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that leaf-level photosynthetic response to CO2 is already included in Earth system models and IPCC WGI technical summaries, but that recognition "does not affect the other clear and staggering harms" of rising greenhouse gases. Do not claim fertilization negates harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of non-CO2 feedbacks that drive warming
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for CO2 feedbacks that drive additional warming through other gases or processes (e.g., methane from wetlands, ice loss, permafrost thaw, soil carbon emissions) that have no fertilization effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many models include CO2 fertilization but omit other feedbacks that generally result in warming; assessments must include these feedbacks because they raise temperatures without impacting CO2 fertilization benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive ocean impacts (warming, stratification, deoxygenation, acidification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess observed impacts of CO2 on oceans largely via ocean warming (heatwaves), stratification and deoxygenation, as well as declines in ocean surface pH (acidification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on ocean acidification; Chapter 2.2's sole focus on pH is a flaw. Consider how warming, stratification, deoxygenation, and acidification act together (historically implicated in mass extinctions) and the particular vulnerability of tropical coral reefs to heat-driven bleaching. Cite observed recent bleaching and reversals of coral cover gains (e.g., 2024 events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of observational detection and regional variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that decreases in ocean surface pH (and other signals) may not yet be uniformly or universally observed and that longer observation periods may be required in some regions for anthropogenic signals to emerge over natural variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite statements such as 'Recent studies indicate that two more decades of observations may be required before anthropogenic ocean acidification emerges over natural variability in some coastal sites and regions.' Use observational-detection caveats appropriately rather than minimizing impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer-reviewed, field-based evidence for CO2 fertilization on crops
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on field studies (e.g., FACE) and meta-analyses rather than greenhouse or open-top chamber (OTC) experiments or non-peer-reviewed sources when estimating realistic CO2 fertilization effects on crop productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis of decades of field studies shows realistic productivity increases roughly half the magnitude of greenhouse/OTC-based estimates. The Draft CWG Report's reliance on greenhouse/OTC numbers (and sources like CO2science.org) is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate CO2 fertilization with direct and indirect climate impacts on agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess agricultural impacts by integrating CO2 fertilization effects with direct impacts (temperature, precipitation) and indirect impacts (pests, pathogens), and consider how these interact (e.g., VPD, drought, water stress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CO2 fertilization is not universal across environments/crop photosynthetic systems; temperature and precipitation changes, vapor pressure deficit increases, drought, and pests/pathogens are major drivers of yield losses and often more consequential than CO2 fertilization. Models must integrate these factors rather than isolate fertilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider water constraints, irrigation limits, and regional hydrology
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate projected changes in precipitation, snowmelt timing, evaporative demand, groundwater decline, and regional water scarcity when assessing agricultural productivity and adaptation capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climate change exacerbates agricultural water scarcity (e.g., U.S. West, Central Valley groundwater decline). Increased irrigation needs and aquifer limits constrain ability to offset warming-induced yield losses; these constraints must be modeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess livestock and farm worker health and productivity impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include heat stress, altered forage and feed costs, flooding impacts, and increased morbidity/mortality among farm workers as part of agricultural/climate impact assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher temperatures reduce livestock welfare and productivity and impose human health burdens (heat stroke, kidney disease, cardiovascular/respiratory exacerbation) on outdoor workers, translating into labor productivity losses and economic costs; include these in impact accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for pest and pathogen dynamics under warming
rubrics_metrics.description: Model and incorporate increased incidence, intensity, and range expansion of pests and pathogens under warming and the consequent crop losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warming increases generations, overwinter survival, and range expansions of pests (e.g., aphids, pink bollworm); empirical studies report substantial crop losses from pests under warming scenarios. Include host- and pest-specific variability in predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include CO2-driven nutritional quality changes (nutrient dilution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how CO2 increases can reduce protein and micronutrient density and alter carbohydrate content in C3 crops, affecting food quality and nutrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analyses and studies (Taub et al. 2008; Loladze 2014; Ainsworth et al. 2025) document reductions in protein and micronutrient density. Even if breeding/GM could mitigate, regional variation and resource requirements mean remedies will lag; account for nutritional impacts and costs to remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective evidence and weak proxies (e.g., farmland value) for yield impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on indirect or selective proxies such as trends in farmland value to infer climate impacts on yields without robust econometric controls for nonfarm influences and complementary crop-yield analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust approaches should integrate crop models, nonlinear yield responses, and farmer decision data; reliance on selective land-value studies or inappropriate citations (e.g., misinterpreting Ortiz-Bobea) can mislead. Account for farmer adaptation drivers and nonfarm influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive economic assessment using the Social Cost of Carbon (SCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SCC-based analyses to estimate welfare impacts of emissions, including health and labor damages not captured by GDP measures, and adopt rigorous, peer-reviewed methods for SCC estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SCC allows quantification of welfare impacts (health, labor) that GDP-based metrics understate; literature and federal guidance support SCC use. SCC estimation should use diverse methodologies (bottom-up, top-down, expert elicitation), report distributions (Monte Carlo), incorporate empirically based health/labor damages, and follow updated discounting guidance (e.g., 2% central real rate per 2023 guidance). Recognize SCC is often a lower-bound because many damages remain unquantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat uncertainty and tail risks explicitly (Monte Carlo, distributions, tipping points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and report uncertainty using Monte Carlo methods, present results as distributions, and explicitly consider tipping points and low-probability high-impact (catastrophic) outcomes in valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty is not a rationale for excluding damages; Monte Carlo linking socioeconomic, climate, and damage modules is standard. Literature (Weitzman and successors) shows small probabilities of extreme warming justify strong action; including tipping points can dramatically increase SCC estimates (6 to 200x in some studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use up-to-date, peer-reviewed evidence and incorporate newly quantified damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously incorporate newly peer-reviewed quantifications of damages (e.g., wildfire smoke mortality) into valuation and impact assessments as they become robust enough for inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCC and impact estimates have risen as newly quantified damages (health costs of wildfire smoke, etc.) are incorporated. Since many impacts remain unquantified, include recent peer-reviewed findings and treat estimates as evolving and generally lower-bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow robust, transparent assessment procedures consistent with IPCC and NCA standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the high-integrity, transparent procedures used by leading scientific assessments (IPCC, NCA) to enhance soundness of conclusions; avoid methods lacking such procedural rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IPCC and NCA are undergirded by robust, transparent procedures; the Draft CWG Report lacks these. Sound assessments should replicate transparency, peer-review, and comprehensive evidence synthesis practices of IPCC/NCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat uncertainty as justification for omission or minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty in quantification does not justify excluding categories of damages or excluding the SCC; policy analysis must incorporate full range of evidence including uncertain but plausible harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous policy requires incorporation of full evidence ranges and uncertainty; omission skews results toward understating risk and understates health and welfare damages.
